correctness.rationale: For a fixed exponent partition, abundancy is maximized by using the smallest available primes, while all assignments of exponents to those primes can be checked exactly. Fresh rational recomputation reproduced the maxima below multiplicity eight, all strictly below four. At multiplicity eight only the partitions \((3,2,1,1,1)\), \((3,1,1,1,1,1)\) and \((2,2,1,1,1,1)\) have maximal abundancy at least four. The inspected verifier performs an exact monotone branch-and-bound over increasing prime assignments; its future-prime abundancy bound is valid and leaves only \(2^3\cdot3^2\cdot5\cdot7\cdot13\), whose divisor sum is exactly four times itself.

originality.rationale: Zhou's complete thesis was materially inspected and explicitly distinguishes \(\omega(N)\), the number of distinct primes, from \(\Omega(N)\), total multiplicity. Its historical section records Carmichael's classifications through five distinct prime factors, including 30240 and 32760, while later chapters study restricted flat/even or odd quadriperfect shapes. Broughan–Zhou prove a strong 22-distinct-prime lower bound only on the odd branch. Flammenkamp's current database reports 'Fewest factors' 8 for abundance 4, but is a computational record rather than an unrestricted proof. No checked source states the submitted all-quadriperfect \(\Omega\ge8\) theorem plus unique equality case.
residual_risks: Older multiply-perfect literature is not uniformly searchable, so an unlinked proof of the same total-multiplicity statement could exist.
The theorem does not classify quadriperfect numbers beyond the boundary layer \(\Omega=8\).
